title: Choosing a Thematic Map
short: Choropleth maps shade areas by a rate, dot maps show where things are, graduated symbols show amounts, isolines join equal values, and cartograms resize places by a number.
trouble: Students shade a choropleth map by raw totals, which makes big areas look important. Choropleth maps should show rates or percentages, such as people per square kilometer.

blocks.html: In Kinds of Maps you met reference maps (where things are) and thematic maps (one topic, such as rainfall). Once you have geographic data, you have to choose how to map it. The right choice depends on what the data measures.

head: Map
How it shows data
Best for
rows: Shades whole areas (states, countries) by a value
Rates and percentages: people per km², percent with internet
One dot stands for a number of things
Where things are: farms, schools, cases of a disease
Totals at points: city populations, port traffic
Lines join places with equal values
Resizes each place by a value

blocks.html: Choose the map from the data: rates on a choropleth, locations as dots, totals as graduated symbols or a cartogram, continuous values as isolines.

blocks.name: humangeo-choro
blocks.cap: The same five regions shaded by total people, then by people per km². Switch and compare.

blocks.html: On a choropleth map the eye reads area: big, dark regions look important. If you shade by totals, large regions get dark just because they are large and hold more people. A rate divides by area (or by population), which removes that size effect, so the shading compares places fairly.

blocks.title: Matching data to maps
blocks.q: Choose a map for each: (a) the number of passengers at 30 airports; (b) the percent of adults with a college degree in each state; (c) average January temperature.
steps: (b) A percentage for each area: a choropleth.
(c) A value that changes smoothly across the land: isolines.

blocks.title: Fixing a map
blocks.q: A student shades U.S. states by total number of farms. Texas is darkest. What is the problem and the fix?
steps: Texas is huge, so it has many farms partly because it has so much land.
Shading by totals makes big states look important.
Fix: shade by a rate (farms per 1,000 km², or percent of land in farms), or show totals with graduated symbols.
blocks.a: Use a rate on the choropleth, or graduated symbols for the totals.

blocks.html: The most common thematic-map mistake is a choropleth of raw totals. Check: does the legend have "per" or "percent" in it? If not, and the map shades areas, it probably should use a rate instead.
